claims.text: Tests are for when the cause isn't clear from history and exam.
claims.quote: Diagnostic tests are indicated when the cause of a skin lesion or disease is not obvious from history and physical examination alone.

claims.text: KOH prep of scale from the lesion's border: hyphae or budding yeast confirm tinea or candidiasis.
claims.quote: For fungal infection, scale is taken from the border of the lesion and placed onto a microscope slide. Then a drop of 10 to 20% potassium hydroxide (KOH) is added. Hyphae, budding yeast, or both confirm the diagnosis of tinea or candidiasis .

claims.text: Scabies scraping: mites, feces or ova confirm it, but a negative scraping does not rule it out.
claims.quote: Findings of mites, feces, or ova confirm the diagnosis. However, a negative scraping does not rule out scabies.

claims.text: Culture of a skin biopsy or vesicle or pustule fluid when infection is suspected.
claims.quote: If an infection is suspected, a sample of material (eg, skin biopsy, vesicular or pustular fluid) may be obtained and sent to a laboratory

claims.text: Punch biopsy samples deep dermal or subcutaneous tissue.
claims.quote: In a punch biopsy, a tubular punch (diameter usually 4 mm) is inserted into deep dermal or subcutaneous tissue to obtain a specimen

claims.text: Shave biopsy suits more superficial lesions.
claims.quote: A shave biopsy is completed with a scalpel or razor blade and may be done for more superficial lesions

claims.text: Tzanck test of an intact vesicle: multinucleated giant cells are a sign of herpes simplex or zoster.
claims.quote: Multinucleated giant cells are a sign of herpes simplex or herpes zoster infection.

claims.text: Diascopy: press a slide on the lesion; hemorrhagic lesions don't blanch, inflammatory and vascular lesions do.
claims.quote: A microscope slide is pressed against a lesion (diascopy) to see whether it blanches. Hemorrhagic lesions do not blanch; inflammatory and vascular lesions do.
